query: If the ticket types that create the heaviest agent workload were reduced, how much would resolution time drop?

per_column.name: category_ticket_volume
per_column.rationale: Volume by category operationalizes 'ticket types that create the heaviest agent workload'; ticket-type mix is an intervenable lever a manager could reduce, so this defines the treatment. It is directly implied by the query.

per_column.name: category_avg_resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: Average resolution time per category is just the focus outcome aggregated; it is the thing being predicted, not a confounder. Named in query as resolution time.

per_column.name: is_heavy_workload_category
per_column.rationale: A binary flag for whether a category is heavy-workload restates the treatment definition ('heaviest agent workload'). Intervenable in principle (reduce those types), but explicitly named in the query.

per_column.name: estimated_resolution_time_hours
per_column.rationale: A per-row estimated resolution time is a projection of the outcome under the intervention; it is all-NULL and adds no adjustment. Not a confounder.

judge.rationale: The added columns identify and operationalize the treatment (heavy-workload ticket categories, an intervenable lever) and restate the outcome, but they contain NO confounders — no common causes of both which categories are heavy and resolution time (e.g., priority, assignment_group capacity/staffing, caller/agent experience, backlog/queue load, time-of-day, category complexity). Without adjusting for such confounders, the counterfactual effect of reducing heavy ticket types on resolution time cannot be identified. The set is essentially a treatment-definition plus outcome restatement, and the outcome projections are empty (all NULL). It fails the decisive test: zero confounders, and none not-already-named in the query. Confounder capability is not demonstrated.
